projects.title: Signup Form: Controlled Inputs and Immutable Updates
projects.tagline: One nested state object, updated correctly — the bug that never shows an error message.
projects.realWorldAnalog: Checkout, onboarding, settings — the majority of real front-end work
projects.architecturePattern: Controlled components over a single nested state object
projects.essence: Build a signup form with nested state (profile, address, preferences), native validation plus custom rules, and a submit that cannot fire twice. The trap is nested updates: mutating one level deep produces a form that stops re-rendering with no error anywhere.
inScope: A real submit with a pending state, a 422 validation response, and no double submit.
A draft restored from storage, and the confirmation screen that renders user input safely.
Every input controlled, including radio, checkbox group, and select.
Nested state updated immutably at two levels of depth.
Native constraint validation plus one rule the browser cannot express.
Labels correctly associated and errors announced with aria-describedby.
outOfScope: A form library — react-hook-form comes after you can do this by hand.

stages.focus: Mutating nested state and uncontrolled inputs
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Typing does nothing. setForm receives the identical object reference, so React bails out of the re-render. No error is thrown — the field simply appears frozen, which is why this bug survives code review.
stages.architecturalLesson: React compares state by reference with Object.is. Mutating in place changes the value but not the identity, so nothing downstream notices.

stages.stageName: New object at every changed level
stages.focus: Copying the path, non-mutating array methods, real validation
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Only the objects on the changed path are recreated; siblings keep their identity, so memoised children below them do not re-render. Errors are associated with their inputs and read out by assistive tech.
stages.architecturalLesson: Immutable update means new identity along the path from root to the change — not a deep clone of everything. sort, splice, push and reverse mutate; map, filter, slice and toSorted do not.

invariants: Every control has an accessible name from a real label element.
No state object is ever mutated; submit is idempotent while pending.

teaches.howCovered: Native constraint validation is used first, with custom rules layered on only where it cannot reach.
The frozen-form bug is reproduced by mutation and fixed by copying each level on the path.

teaches.subtopic: Object references, shallow copies and deep cloning
teaches.howCovered: Spread is shown to be shallow, and structuredClone is contrasted with a hand-written deep copy.

implicitFoundations.title: Reference identity
implicitFoundations.mechanism: Objects are compared by reference; a shallow spread copies one level and shares the rest.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: The single most common source of "React is not updating" bug reports.

implicitFoundations.title: Native form submission
implicitFoundations.mechanism: A form submits on Enter within a text field and serialises named controls.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Explains why a div with a click handler is not a form.

manualEngineeringRequired: Immutable nested updates without an immer-style helper.
Error announcement wiring.

uses.why: Native constraint validation is used first, and custom rules are added only where the browser cannot express them
The mutation that freezes the form with no error is reproduced, then fixed by copying every level on the path
Spread is shown to be shallow, then contrasted with structuredClone and a hand-written deep copy
Nested updates use the updater form, since several fields can change before a single re-render commits
The checkbox group is maintained with filter and spread, and push, splice and sort are named as the mutating set
Restoring and saving the draft is synchronisation with an external store, debounced and cleaned up
The draft persists to localStorage, and the JSON round-trip losing undefined and Dates is met head on
Submission is async with a pending state, and a double submit must be impossible while the first is in flight
POST is not idempotent, so retry policy and a 422 validation response are both handled deliberately
User input is rendered back on the confirmation screen, which is where XSS is demonstrated and then prevented
Errors are associated with aria-describedby and announced, and focus moves to the first invalid control on submit
The form shape is one type, and the errors map is derived from it so a renamed field breaks the compile
A restored field must default with ?? or a legitimately empty string is replaced by a placeholder
Every input value is a string, so the age field needs an explicit conversion with a stated NaN policy
Deciding whether the form is dirty is a sameness question, and === on objects always answers false
A boundary wraps the form so a render failure shows a recoverable message instead of a blank page
Field, Label and Error compose as a compound component sharing the field id implicitly
useRef holds the node to focus after a failed submit, and useReducer replaces four correlated flags
The debounced saver closes over the latest form snapshot, which is where a stale draft comes from
The pending flag must be set before the await, or a fast double click starts two requests
Rules are methods on a validator object, so passing one as a callback loses its receiver unless it is bound

fieldset and legend group the related controls, which is what makes the radio group announce as a group

Invalid, focused and disabled each need a visible state that is not carried by colour alone
:focus-within highlights the whole field group, and :user-invalid avoids shouting before the user has finished
Each field is a column of label, control and error, which is a one-axis layout
The address block is a small grid so the postcode and city do not need one-off widths
Validation rules live in their own module so they can be reused by the tests in a later project
The debounce is written by hand, including the cancel that stops a save after unmount

projects.title: Fetch a List: Loading, Error, Empty, Data
projects.tagline: The four states, a race condition, and an abort — in about a hundred lines.
projects.realWorldAnalog: Every list screen in every product
projects.architecturePattern: Component-owned async state with an AbortController
projects.essence: Fetch and render a searchable list. The interesting part is not the happy path — it is the request that resolves after a newer one, the error that leaves a spinner running forever, and the empty result that renders as a blank screen. All three are graded in a real machine-coding round.
inScope: A cross-origin endpoint, so preflight and the opaque failure are met rather than read about.
A cached last-good response with a visible staleness marker for offline reloads.
All four view states rendered distinctly: loading, error, empty, data.
A debounced search that cancels the in-flight request with AbortController.
Correct handling of a non-2xx response — fetch does not reject on 404.
A retry that clears the previous error.
outOfScope: TanStack Query or SWR — write it once by hand first.
A backend; a public API or a mocked delay is enough.

stages.focus: One boolean, no cancellation, no status check
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Typing "react" fires five requests; whichever resolves last wins, so results can belong to "rea". fetch resolves for a 404, so an error page is rendered as data. An empty array renders as a blank screen with no explanation.
stages.architecturalLesson: fetch rejects only on network failure. Response.ok is the check, and out-of-order resolution is a correctness bug, not a performance one.

stages.focus: AbortController, status checks, a discriminated state union
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Only the newest request can write state, because the effect cleanup aborts the previous one. A 404 lands in the error branch. Empty and error are distinct screens, so a user never sees an unexplained blank list.
stages.architecturalLesson: Modelling async as one union — loading | error | empty | data — makes impossible combinations unrepresentable. Two booleans allow four states, of which two are nonsense.

invariants: Exactly one of the four states renders at a time.
No response from a superseded request may write state.

teaches.subtopic: HTTP, status codes, methods and idempotency
teaches.howCovered: Response.ok and status branching are written by hand, including 4xx vs 5xx retry policy.
The race is reproduced, then removed with AbortController wired to the effect cleanup.
Cleanup is used as the cancellation point, which is the canonical answer to the stale-response question.

implicitFoundations.title: Request lifecycle
implicitFoundations.mechanism: DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP round trips precede the first byte of the response body.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Explains why a spinner appears before any data can possibly arrive.

implicitFoundations.title: Microtask ordering
implicitFoundations.mechanism: Promise callbacks run on the microtask queue, draining before the next macrotask.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Explains the exact interleaving of two in-flight requests resolving.

manualEngineeringRequired: Cancellation, status handling and the state union — no data library allowed.
A debounce written from scratch.

uses.why: The out-of-order race is reproduced, then removed with an AbortController wired into the effect cleanup
Response.ok, 4xx versus 5xx retry policy and idempotency are each decided by hand rather than by a library default
Cleanup is the cancellation point, which is the canonical answer to the stale-response interview question
The third-party endpoint triggers a preflight, and the opaque failure is diagnosed from the network panel, not guessed
Two in-flight requests resolving on the microtask queue is what makes the last-writer-wins bug deterministic to demonstrate
The four states are one discriminated union, so a loading-and-error combination cannot be constructed
The last successful response is cached so an offline reload shows data with an explicit staleness marker
Result text comes from a third party, so escaping and a URL-scheme allowlist for result links are required
The debounce is written from scratch, including cancel, because the search fires on every keystroke
Each effect run closes over its own controller, which is precisely why the stale one can be aborted
Results are mapped and filtered into view models without mutating the fetched payload
State transitions go through a reducer, since four states with typed payloads outgrow four useState calls
useReducer models the state machine and useRef holds the controller, neither of which should trigger a render
Keys on result rows decide whether state follows the item or the position when results change
A boundary catches a render failure on malformed data so the whole page does not go blank
Spinner, ErrorPanel, EmptyState and ResultList are swapped behind one interface by the state union
Optional fields in the payload default with ?? so a legitimate 0 rating is not shown as unrated
Query params are strings, so page and limit need explicit conversion before they are used as numbers
Deciding whether a cached response matches the current query is a stated sameness rule, not a === on objects
The cached array is copied before it is handed out, so a consumer cannot corrupt the cache in place
The fetch wrapper is its own module, which is what makes it mockable at a boundary in the testing project
Marking a row as read produces a new array, which is what lets a memoised row skip re-rendering
Loading, error and empty are announced through a live region, since a visual-only spinner tells a screen reader nothing
Results are a list and the search is a form with role="search", which is what makes the region navigable
The search input is a real form control with a label, so Enter submits and the field is announced
The pending state needs to be visible without the layout jumping when results replace the skeleton
Skeleton rows reserve their final height with aspect-ratio so the list does not shift when data lands
Each result row is a flex line with a growing title and a trailing meta column
The scroll container needs its own formatting context or the sticky search header escapes it
DNS, TLS and the first byte all precede any data, which is why the spinner exists at all

projects.title: The Class Component Museum: Port It Twice
projects.tagline: The same widget as a class and as a hook — because the assessment still asks about both.
projects.realWorldAnalog: Any codebase older than 2019, which is most of them
projects.architecturePattern: Parallel implementations: lifecycle methods vs hooks
projects.essence: Write one widget twice — once with componentDidMount / componentDidUpdate / componentWillUnmount, once with hooks — and map each method to its hook equivalent. Mettl publishes "Lifecycle" as a named React sub-skill, and enterprise React codebases still contain thousands of class components. This is also the cleanest place to meet the prototype chain, since a class is one.
inScope: A withSubscription HOC, then the same behaviour as a custom hook.
A real async load, which the class version must cancel in componentWillUnmount.
A subscription widget implemented as a class and as a function component.
A mapping table from each lifecycle method to its hook equivalent.
One error boundary — still only expressible as a class.
Inspecting the prototype chain of the class instance in devtools.
outOfScope: Legacy UNSAFE_ lifecycle methods beyond naming them.

stages.stageName: The class, with its classic bugs
stages.focus: Lifecycle methods, bound handlers, setState merging
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: tick throws because a class method passed as a callback loses its receiver. setState merges at the top level only, so setting { meta: {...} } replaces the whole nested object. Setup and teardown live in three separate methods, so one is routinely forgotten.
stages.architecturalLesson: Class components split one concern across three lifecycle methods. That separation, not verbosity, is the reason hooks exist.

stages.stageName: The same widget, as one effect
stages.focus: Mapping lifecycle to hooks and reading the prototype chain
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: One effect replaces three lifecycle methods, and the dependency array makes the didUpdate condition declarative. Instance state stays on the instance; methods live on the prototype and are shared across every instance.
stages.architecturalLesson: `class` is syntax over prototypes. Knowing where a method actually lives explains method sharing, `super`, and why an arrow class field is per-instance.

invariants: Every lifecycle method used is paired with its hook equivalent in the table.
Setup and its teardown are never more than a few lines apart.

teaches.subtopic: Class components and the lifecycle vocabulary
teaches.howCovered: Every common lifecycle method is written, then mapped to its hook equivalent in a table you build.

teaches.subtopic: Prototypes, the prototype chain and classes
teaches.howCovered: The class instance is walked with getPrototypeOf to show where methods and state actually live.
An error boundary is implemented — the one thing that still requires a class in React 19.

implicitFoundations.title: Method binding
implicitFoundations.mechanism: A prototype method has no bound receiver; a class field arrow captures the instance at construction.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Explains the constructor .bind(this) lines in every legacy React file.

manualEngineeringRequired: The lifecycle-to-hook mapping, written from understanding rather than copied.

projects.title: A Real Multi-page SPA: Routes, Params and Guards
projects.tagline: Four screens, nested layouts, a protected route, and a URL you can actually share.
projects.realWorldAnalog: The shell of any dashboard product
projects.architecturePattern: Nested route tree with layout routes and a guard wrapper
projects.essence: Assemble the previous projects into one application behind a router: a list screen, a detail screen driven by a URL parameter, a form screen, and a protected area. The lesson is that the URL is state — if a filter or an open tab is not in the URL, a shared link does not reproduce the screen.
inScope: Route-level code splitting, and the catch-all rewrite a deep link needs.
A small shared store for the session, kept deliberately separate from URL state.
Nested layout routes with a shared shell and an Outlet.
A dynamic :id route reading params, plus search params for filters.
A guarded route that redirects and returns the user to their target after login.
A 404 route and an error element.
outOfScope: A real auth backend — a boolean in state is enough.
Server-side rendering or data loaders beyond one example.

stages.focus: A page variable and filters that vanish on reload
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: The back button leaves the app entirely. A link to a detail screen cannot be shared — it always opens the list. Reloading resets the filter. Every new screen adds another branch to the ternary chain.
stages.architecturalLesson: Navigation state that lives in a component is invisible to the browser. The address bar is the oldest state container on the platform.

stages.focus: Nested routes, params, search params, guarded redirect
stages.codeSnippet:
<Route element={<AppShell />}>            {/* layout route */}
  <Route path="items" element={<List />} />
  <Route path="items/:id" element={<Detail />} />
  <Route element={<RequireAuth />}>       {/* guard wraps children */}
    <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
  </Route>
  <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
</Route>

const { id } = useParams();
const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams();  // filter is shareable
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Back and forward work. A pasted URL reproduces the exact screen including filters. The guard redirects to login and returns to the original destination afterwards rather than dumping the user on the home page.
stages.architecturalLesson: A route tree is composition: layout routes provide the shell, guard routes provide the policy, and leaf routes provide the screen. The same idea as children and wrapper components, expressed as a data structure.

invariants: Every navigable screen has a URL; no screen is reachable only by button.
Shell chrome is written once and shared by every route beneath it.

projects.title: Write Redux Yourself, Then Delete It
projects.tagline: Forty lines of createStore, then the same app on Redux Toolkit — and you can defend both.
projects.realWorldAnalog: The state layer of any enterprise React application
projects.architecturePattern: Unidirectional data flow: dispatcher → store → view
projects.essence: Implement a working store — subscribe, dispatch, getState, a reducer, and a middleware chain — in about forty lines, then rebuild the same feature on Redux Toolkit. Mettl bills Redux at parity with React itself on its React assessment, and Flux appears by name on the ReactJS paper; almost no 2026 preparation material covers either.
inScope: createStore with getState, dispatch, subscribe and replaceReducer.
combineReducers and one applyMiddleware chain including a logger and a thunk.
The same feature ported to configureStore and createSlice.
One memoised selector, and a demonstration of what it stops re-rendering.
outOfScope: A normalised entity cache beyond one small example.
Server state — that belongs to TanStack Query, and the project says why.

stages.focus: Dispatcher, multiple stores, emitted change events
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Stores mutate private arrays and emit an untyped change event, so a view knows something changed but not what. Cross-store dependencies need waitFor with explicit dispatch tokens, and the order becomes load-bearing.
stages.architecturalLesson: Flux got the direction right — one way, always — and the storage wrong. Redux keeps the direction and replaces N mutable stores with one immutable tree.

stages.focus: Pure reducers, subscription, middleware as function composition
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: A reducer that mutates state or reads Date.now() breaks time-travel debugging and makes tests flaky. A subscriber that dispatches during notification recurses.
stages.architecturalLesson: The three Redux rules — single source of truth, read-only state, changes via pure functions — are what make the devtools, replay and undo possible. They are constraints that buy capabilities.

stages.stageName: Redux Toolkit, understood rather than copied
stages.focus: createSlice, Immer drafts, thunks, memoised selectors
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: state.push looks like mutation and is not — Immer records the draft operations and produces a new tree. A selector returning a fresh array literal each call re-renders every subscriber; createSelector is what stops it.
stages.architecturalLesson: RTK removes boilerplate, not concepts. You still have to know that the reducer is pure, or the draft syntax will mislead you in code review.

invariants: A reducer is a pure function of (state, action) with no I/O.
All side effects live in middleware, never in a reducer.
A component subscribes to the narrowest slice it can.

teaches.subtopic: Store, actions, reducers, pure functions, data flow
teaches.howCovered: createStore is implemented from scratch, so every one of the five terms is code you wrote.

teaches.subtopic: react-redux, middleware, thunks and Redux Toolkit
teaches.howCovered: The hand-built store is replaced by configureStore and createSlice with the same feature behaviour.

teaches.subtopic: Flux — and why Mettl still asks about it
teaches.howCovered: The original dispatcher-and-stores design is built first, so the Redux comparison is first-hand.

teaches.subtopic: Context, Zustand, TanStack Query — picking the tool
teaches.howCovered: Ends with an explicit written argument for which of the four this feature should have used.

implicitFoundations.title: Closures as private state
implicitFoundations.mechanism: createStore keeps state and listeners in closure scope rather than on an object.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: The store is unreachable except through its three methods — encapsulation without classes.

implicitFoundations.title: Structural sharing
implicitFoundations.mechanism: Immutable updates copy only the path to the change, leaving siblings referentially equal.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Makes shallow reference comparison a sufficient re-render check for a large tree.

manualEngineeringRequired: The store, the middleware chain and the selector memoisation, written before importing any of them.
The written justification for the final choice of tool.

projects.title: The Utility Belt: Implement Lodash, Badly, Then Correctly
projects.tagline: debounce, throttle, curry, deepClone, Promise.all, and a bind that handles `new`.
projects.realWorldAnalog: The 45-minute machine-coding round
projects.architecturePattern: A published-shaped module with tests for the edge cases
projects.essence: Implement the functions interviewers ask you to implement live: debounce with leading and trailing options, throttle, curry, deep clone with cycles, a bind that survives `new`, and Promise.all/allSettled/race from scratch. Each one is a closure, a `this` rule or a microtask rule that you can then explain rather than recall.
inScope: debounce (leading/trailing/maxWait) and throttle, with cancel and flush.
curry supporting placeholders and variadic arity.
deepClone handling cycles, Map, Set, Date and RegExp.
myBind, myCall, myApply — including the `new` case — and Promise combinators.
outOfScope: A build pipeline; one ESM module with tests is the deliverable.

stages.stageName: The version that passes the demo
stages.focus: Naive implementations that break on the second question
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: debounce drops the receiver and every argument, so a debounced method call fails. The JSON clone silently corrupts Dates, undefined, Map, Set and NaN, and throws outright on a cycle.
stages.architecturalLesson: These are the follow-up questions, not gotchas. The interviewer asks "what about `this`?" because that is where the understanding is.

stages.focus: Preserved receiver and arguments, cycle-safe cloning, spec-shaped combinators
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: The debounced function forwards `this` and every argument, supports cancel, and does not fire a trailing call after cancel. deepClone terminates on a self-referencing object because a WeakMap remembers what it has already copied.
stages.architecturalLesson: A WeakMap is the right cycle registry precisely because it does not retain its keys — the clone does not leak the source graph.

stages.focus: all, allSettled, race, any — and why ordering is preserved
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Using push instead of an index returns results in completion order, which is the single most common bug in this exercise. Forgetting the empty-iterable case leaves the promise pending forever.
stages.architecturalLesson: Writing the combinator makes the microtask queue concrete: every .then callback is a microtask, and they drain before the next timer fires.

invariants: Every timing utility exposes cancel; none leaks a pending timer.
Receiver and arity are preserved through every wrapper.
Result order matches input order regardless of settle order.

teaches.subtopic: Polyfills, debounce, throttle, curry, deep clone

projects.title: A Component Library You Can Defend in Review
projects.tagline: Six components, generic props, tests that survive a refactor, and a keyboard that works.
projects.realWorldAnalog: The internal design-system package at any mid-size company
projects.architecturePattern: Headless behaviour hooks + presentational components
projects.essence: Build Button, Dialog, Combobox, Tabs, Toast and DataList as a properly typed package with tests. The discriminating skill is not writing them — it is writing tests that fail when the behaviour breaks and pass when the markup is refactored, and typing a polymorphic component without reaching for any.
inScope: Six components split into a behaviour hook and a presentational shell.
Generic and polymorphic props typed without any, including an `as` prop.
Tests written against role and accessible name, never against class names.
Full keyboard support per the WAI-ARIA authoring practices for each pattern.
outOfScope: Storybook, visual regression, or a docs site.

stages.stageName: Components that pass their own tests
stages.focus: any-typed props and tests bound to implementation details
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Renaming .btn-primary breaks a test that has nothing to do with the change, so the suite gets ignored. Meanwhile the dialog is a div with no role, no focus trap and no Escape handler — and every test passes.
stages.architecturalLesson: A test coupled to markup measures the markup. A test coupled to role and accessible name measures what a user — and a screen reader — can actually do.

stages.focus: Headless hooks, discriminated props, role-based queries
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: The test now fails if focus is not moved into the dialog or Escape stops working, and survives a full CSS rewrite. Polymorphic props are inferred, so <Button as="a" href=...> type-checks and <Button as="a" type="submit"> does not.
stages.architecturalLesson: Separating behaviour from presentation is what makes both testable in isolation — and it is the same reason headless libraries exist.

stages.focus: Mocking the network, not the module under test
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Mocking the component’s own fetch wrapper makes the test pass even when the real request shape is wrong. Intercepting at the network boundary tests the code that will actually run in production.
stages.architecturalLesson: Mock at a boundary you do not own. Everything inside the boundary should be exercised for real, or the test is checking your mock.

invariants: No hook renders DOM; each returns prop getters.
Every interactive element is reachable and operable by keyboard alone.
No `any` in any exported type.

projects.title: Design It On The Whiteboard, Then Actually Build It
projects.tagline: A dashboard specified as a design document first — components, data, states, failure.
projects.realWorldAnalog: The front-end system design round at any 2-5 YOE interview
projects.architecturePattern: Server-state / client-state separation with an explicit failure policy
projects.essence: Write the design document first — component boundaries, data flow, every state, and what happens when each dependency fails — then build exactly what the document specifies. The round is graded on whether you volunteered the failure modes, and this is the only way to practise that rather than read about it.
inScope: A written design doc: component tree, data ownership, state inventory, failure table.
Server state in a query cache; client state kept separate and small.
Offline-tolerant reads from IndexedDB with an explicit staleness indicator.
A degraded mode: one widget fails without taking the page down.
outOfScope: A charting library beyond one chart.

stages.focus: One global store holding everything, no failure policy
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Promise.all means one slow or failing endpoint blanks the whole dashboard. Server data and UI flags share a store, so a refetch invalidates the sidebar state. Nobody can say what the screen shows when the feed is empty but the KPIs loaded.
stages.architecturalLesson: Server state and client state have different lifetimes, different invalidation rules and different owners. Merging them makes both harder.

stages.focus: State inventory, per-widget boundaries, an explicit failure table
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Each widget owns its own request, boundary and skeleton, so a failing feed shows one degraded card rather than a blank page. Every cell of the failure table corresponds to code that exists.
stages.architecturalLesson: The failure table is the deliverable interviewers actually want. Producing it unprompted is the difference between a mid-level and a senior answer.

stages.focus: Stale-while-revalidate, IndexedDB persistence, cache invalidation rules
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: A user opening the dashboard offline sees yesterday’s numbers clearly labelled as stale, rather than either a spinner forever or stale numbers presented as current.
stages.architecturalLesson: Showing cached data is a product decision as much as a technical one. The honest version tells the user how old the number is.

invariants: No component is written before its row exists in the state inventory.
Server state never lives in the client store, and vice versa.
A single widget failure never blanks the page.

implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: An application cache that ignores the transport cache does the same work twice.

implicitFoundations.title: What may be persisted
implicitFoundations.mechanism: Anything in IndexedDB or localStorage is readable by script on that origin.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Rules out persisting tokens, and explains the httpOnly cookie recommendation.

The offline persistence layer and staleness surfacing.

projects.title: The Performance Autopsy: Measure Before You Memo
projects.tagline: A deliberately slow gallery, a profile, and only the fixes the profile justified.
projects.realWorldAnalog: The quarterly Core Web Vitals regression nobody wants to own
projects.architecturePattern: Measured optimisation: profile, hypothesis, change, re-measure
projects.essence: Take a 5,000-item image gallery that renders badly, profile it, and fix only what the measurements identify. Half the candidates who reach for useMemo cannot say what it cost or what it saved; this project requires a before-and-after number for every optimisation, and reverting any change that did not earn its place.
inScope: A React Profiler trace and a Performance panel trace, before and after.
List virtualisation, with the row count and frame time recorded either side.
Route-level code splitting with a measured entry-bundle delta.
LCP, CLS and INP measured on a throttled profile, not on your laptop.
outOfScope: Optimising anything the profile did not flag.

stages.focus: memo everywhere, no measurement
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: memo compares props shallowly and the inline arrow is a new reference every render, so all 5,000 rows re-render anyway — now with an added comparison cost. Images without dimensions produce a CLS of 0.4.
stages.architecturalLesson: memo is a shallow prop comparison. It is defeated by any new object, array or function identity passed as a prop, which is most props.

stages.focus: Reading a flame chart and naming the actual cost
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Virtualisation cuts the commit from 412ms to 8ms; the memo wrappers, re-measured, save nothing and are removed. The number, not the instinct, decided which change stayed.
stages.architecturalLesson: Optimisation is a hypothesis with a measurement on either side. A change with no before-and-after number is a guess that also increased complexity.

stages.focus: Code splitting, image sizing, and the critical path
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Entry bundle falls from 495kB to 69kB and LCP from 4.1s to 1.6s on a throttled profile. CLS goes to 0 because every image reserves its box before it loads.
stages.architecturalLesson: Rendering performance and loading performance are different problems with different tools. Web Vitals separate them for exactly that reason.

invariants: Every optimisation has a recorded before and after number.
No memo survives that did not change a measurement.
Every image reserves its space before it loads.

teaches.howCovered: Each tool is applied, measured, and reverted if the measurement did not justify it.

implicitFoundations.title: Long tasks and the main thread
implicitFoundations.mechanism: Any task over 50ms blocks input handling until it yields.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Directly explains a poor INP score and why virtualisation improved responsiveness.

implicitFoundations.title: Allocation pressure
implicitFoundations.mechanism: Objects allocated per render are collected in the young generation, pausing the main thread.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Explains why stable identities help beyond just satisfying memo.

Minimal scope (4 layout primitives, dynamic remote loader, action bus) with maximum architectural depth: Zod AST validation, Module Federation 2.0 with SRI, and CSS Subgrid multi-card alignment.
inScope: Server-driven layout stream parsing 4 core primitives (Hero, Carousel, BentoGrid, ActionCard).
Module Federation 2.0 dynamic remote loader with SRI validation.
Declarative Command Bus for server actions (NAVIGATE, MODAL, MUTATE).
CSS Subgrid multi-card baseline alignment with @container queries.

stages.focus: Naïve Switch Statement & Dynamic Script Tag
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Backend introducing a new component type before client release crashes the parser. Unsandboxed script tags allow rogue micro-frontends to crash the entire host app.
stages.architecturalLesson: Server-Driven UI requires recursive schema validation with graceful unknown node fallbacks, and micro-frontends require isolated error boundaries.

stages.focus: Layout Shift (CLS) & Detached DOM Memory Leaks
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Remote components loading asynchronously cause severe Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). Unmounted micro-apps leak window listeners and detached DOM trees.
stages.architecturalLesson: Micro-frontends must enforce strict layout sizing reservations and explicit teardown lifecycles.

stages.focus: Recursive Zod AST Schema + Module Federation 2.0 with SRI + RSC
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Zero client crashes on unknown server types. Federated remotes are verified with cryptographic SRI hashes and isolated by ErrorBoundaries.
stages.architecturalLesson: Type-safe AST contracts and dependency sandboxing enable bulletproof enterprise server-driven architectures.

stages.focus: CSS Subgrid Baseline Alignment, Container Queries & Telemetry
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Card headers, bodies, and CTAs align perfectly across dynamic server columns. Telemetry flushes reliably on page unload.
stages.architecturalLesson: Subgrid and container queries guarantee visual elegance for dynamically generated layouts.

invariants: Remote crashes are isolated by ErrorBoundary wrappers without breaking parent layout.
All server-driven actions pass through a centralized command bus.
Zod runtime validation guarantees client contract safety before rendering.
Shared singletons (React, QueryClient) deduplicated across remote micro-apps.

projects.title: ChronosGraph: Local-First Knowledge IDE with WebGPU & CRDTs

projects.realWorldAnalog: Obsidian / Notion / Roam Research Core
projects.architecturePattern: Local-First Clean Architecture + CRDT DAG + WebGPU Compute
projects.essence: Build a local-first personal knowledge management IDE operating with zero network latency. Minimal scope (Markdown editor, 100k-node graph, offline CRDT sync) with maximum architectural depth: OPFS SyncAccessHandle, WebGPU WGSL compute shaders, and TanStack Query offline persistence.

stages.focus: Main-Thread LocalStorage & D3 SVG Graph
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: D3 CPU force simulation chokes at >2,000 nodes, dropping framerates to <1 FPS. Serializing vaults to localStorage freezes user typing.
stages.architecturalLesson: O(N^2) graph layout physics cannot run on the CPU main thread. Storage and compute must be offloaded to dedicated workers and GPU kernels.

stages.focus: Offline Sync Race Conditions & Stored XSS
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Reconnecting after offline editing causes silent data overwrites. Raw markdown parsing allows malicious script injections in shared vaults.
stages.architecturalLesson: Local-first architecture requires state-based CRDTs for deterministic convergence and AST-level sanitization for zero-trust security.

stages.focus: WebGPU WGSL Compute + OPFS SyncAccessHandle + Yjs CRDT
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: 100,000 graph nodes run at steady 60 FPS on GPU. Synchronous OPFS file access handles eliminate IndexedDB IPC serialization latency.
stages.architecturalLesson: WebGPU compute passes unlock desktop-grade data scale; OPFS provides native file system streaming in the browser.

stages.focus: CSS Subgrid Outliner, AST Sanitization & Storage Quota
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Knowledge outliner rows stay perfectly aligned across nested depths. Persistent storage quota prevents browser eviction.
stages.architecturalLesson: Production local-first apps must defend persistence guarantees with navigator.storage.persist() and AST sanitizers.

projects.realWorldAnalog: Figma / Miro / Excalidraw Core Engine
projects.architecturePattern: Clean Hexagonal + CQRS + Entity-Component System (ECS)
projects.essence: Build a high-performance infinite whiteboard handling 50,000+ vector shapes with sub-16ms latency. Minimal feature breadth (no auth, no billing, no menu bloat) with maximum architectural depth: WebGL2 OffscreenCanvas, BVH spatial indexing, binary WebSocket sync, and local-first CRDTs.
inScope: 50,000 vector shapes on an infinite pan/zoom canvas.

stages.focus: Main-Thread React State Canvas
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Main-thread loop over 50,000 shapes takes 180ms per frame. Frame rate drops to 5 FPS with catastrophic INP jank (>200ms).
stages.architecturalLesson: Direct React state mutation cannot scale to high-frequency vector manipulation. UI state must be decoupled from the rendering pipeline.

stages.focus: OffscreenCanvas WebGL2 Worker + BVH Spatial Index + Binary CRDT
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Rendering is offloaded 100% to Web Workers. BVH culls 49,900 offscreen shapes in O(log N) time, locking framerate at a steady 120 FPS.
stages.architecturalLesson: Leverage WebGL2 instancing, off-main-thread compute, and binary state vectors for institutional-scale graphics.

stages.focus: CSS Subgrid Inspector, Virtual A11y Tree & Float32 Pooling
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Zero layout shift across nested property inputs. Screen readers navigate hidden AOM mirror with full ARIA semantics.
stages.architecturalLesson: True masterclass engineering combines raw performance with polished UI design systems and WCAG accessibility.

invariants: Zero main-thread vector drawing; UI renders only chrome and tools.
O(log N) frustum culling before dispatching draw calls.

Zero heap allocations during steady-state 120 FPS loops.

projects.title: A Plugin Runtime That Executes Code You Do Not Trust
projects.tagline: Third-party plugins, in your page, with your user session — and no path to their data.
projects.realWorldAnalog: Figma plugins / Shopify checkout extensions
projects.architecturePattern: Capability-based sandbox: null-origin iframe + worker + RPC membrane
projects.essence: Build a runtime that lets untrusted plugin code render UI and call host APIs, where a hostile plugin cannot read the session, exfiltrate data, or freeze the page. The security model is the entire project: every capability a plugin holds must be one you deliberately handed it, and the interesting failures are the ones that look safe.
inScope: Plugin execution in a null-origin sandboxed iframe hosting a Worker.
A structured RPC membrane — no host object ever crosses the boundary.
A capability manifest: a plugin receives exactly the APIs it declared.
A watchdog that terminates a plugin exceeding its time or memory budget.
outOfScope: A plugin marketplace, billing, or review pipeline.
A custom JavaScript interpreter — the platform already isolates.

stages.focus: Running plugin code in the host realm
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: The plugin has the host origin, so it holds the session cookie, localStorage, the DOM and every fetch credential. An infinite loop freezes the main thread. Freezing prototypes does not help — the plugin can reach the same globals through any object it is handed.
stages.architecturalLesson: Isolation is a property of the realm and the origin, not of how carefully you pass objects. Same realm means no isolation at all.

stages.focus: Null-origin iframe, worker realm, CSP, postMessage only
stages.codeSnippet:
<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"          <!-- no allow-same-origin: null origin -->
        csp="default-src 'none'; script-src 'unsafe-inline'"
        src="data:text/html,..."></iframe>

// Inside: the plugin runs in a Worker, so it cannot touch even that DOM
worker.postMessage({ type: 'render', props: structuredClone(safeProps) });
// structuredClone throws on functions — accidental capability leaks fail loudly
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: The plugin realm has a null origin, so it shares no storage, no cookies and no DOM with the host. A runaway loop blocks only its own worker thread. Crucially, `allow-scripts` together with `allow-same-origin` would silently undo all of this — the two flags together are equivalent to no sandbox.
stages.architecturalLesson: structuredClone as the only transport is a design choice, not a limitation: if a value cannot be cloned it cannot be a capability leak.

stages.focus: A membrane that hands out revocable, narrow references
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: A plugin granted storage:read for `prefs` cannot read `session` by passing a different key, because the grant validates arguments and not merely the method name. Revoking a grant takes effect on the next call with no plugin cooperation.
stages.architecturalLesson: A permission is a question asked at the boundary; a capability is an unforgeable reference. Capabilities compose and revoke cleanly, which is why every real plugin system converges on them.

stages.focus: Watchdogs, rendering untrusted trees, telemetry per plugin
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: A plugin returning a node with an onClick string, a javascript: href, or an unknown type is rejected at the schema rather than rendered. A plugin missing its 32ms frame budget is terminated and shown as degraded, not allowed to drop frames for everyone.
stages.architecturalLesson: Untrusted UI is data describing a tree, never markup. The host decides what a described node is permitted to become.

invariants: No host object reference ever crosses the postMessage boundary.
allow-scripts and allow-same-origin are never set together.
A plugin holds only capabilities its manifest declared and the user approved.

teaches.howCovered: The threat model is written first; CSP, sandbox flags and URL-scheme validation are each defeated then fixed.
The null-origin iframe makes the same-origin policy the enforcement mechanism rather than a footnote.
Demonstrates that a null-origin frame shares no cookies, localStorage or IndexedDB with the host.
structuredClone is used as the only transport precisely because it cannot carry a function.

teaches.subtopic: Runtime validation at a trust boundary
teaches.howCovered: Every inbound message is schema-parsed, since a type annotation is erased and proves nothing at runtime.

implicitFoundations.title: Realms and origins
implicitFoundations.mechanism: Each browsing context has its own realm and intrinsics; the origin tuple gates storage and DOM access.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Explains why object-freezing defences fail and platform isolation does not.

implicitFoundations.title: Thread isolation
implicitFoundations.mechanism: A Worker has its own event loop and heap; terminate() reclaims both immediately.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: A hostile infinite loop costs one worker rather than the user’s tab.

manualEngineeringRequired: The capability registry, the membrane and the revocation model.
The threat model document, written before any code.
Schema validation of every untrusted UI tree.

projects.title: Write React: Fiber, Hooks and a Reconciler of Your Own
projects.tagline: A working renderer with interruptible rendering and a real hook dispatcher, in one repo.
projects.realWorldAnalog: React’s own reconciler package
projects.architecturePattern: Fiber linked list + work loop + double buffering + hook slot array
projects.essence: Implement a renderer: JSX to elements, elements to a fiber tree, a work loop that yields to the browser, a commit phase, and hooks backed by a per-fiber slot array. Once you have written the dispatcher, every hook rule stops being a rule you memorised and becomes an obvious consequence of an array and an index.
inScope: createElement, a fiber tree, and a work loop driven by a deadline.
Reconciliation by type and key, with placement, update and deletion effects.
useState and useEffect backed by a hook slot array on the fiber.
A commit phase separated from render, with double buffering.
outOfScope: Concurrent lanes, transitions and Suspense — name them, do not build them.
Matching React’s API surface beyond the four exports above.

stages.focus: Straight recursion into the DOM
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: A 10,000-node tree blocks the main thread for the entire traversal, so no input is handled until it finishes. Because the DOM is mutated during traversal, an error halfway leaves a half-built UI on screen.
stages.architecturalLesson: Recursion cannot be interrupted — the call stack is the traversal state. Making rendering pausable requires the traversal state to live in a data structure you control.

stages.focus: A linked list, a unit of work, and yielding to the browser
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: Rendering yields between fibers, so typing stays responsive during a large update. Nothing reaches the DOM until the whole tree is ready, so a partial tree is never visible.
stages.architecturalLesson: The render phase is pure and interruptible; the commit phase is synchronous and cannot be. That split is the reason effects run when they do.

stages.focus: Diffing by type and key, alternate fibers, double buffering
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: With index keys, reordering a list of inputs leaves the typed values attached to the wrong rows — the fiber matched by position, so state stayed with position. With stable keys the state follows the item.
stages.architecturalLesson: The key is what tells the reconciler that two fibers across renders are the same thing. Every "why is my list state wrong" bug is this one sentence.

stages.focus: A slot array indexed by call order
stages.failureModeOrInvariant: A hook inside an `if` shifts every subsequent index, so useState(2) reads the slot belonging to useEffect. The state does not just go wrong — it becomes a different hook’s state.
stages.architecturalLesson: The rules of hooks are not a style guide. Call order is the only identity a hook has, and this is why `use()` — which is not slot-backed — is the one hook allowed to be conditional.

invariants: An element is an immutable description; it holds no DOM node.
The render phase performs no DOM mutation and may be abandoned at any point.
Commit is synchronous and applies the whole tree or none of it.
Hook order is identical on every render of a given fiber.

teaches.subtopic: Fiber, the work loop, double buffering and reconciliation
teaches.howCovered: The fiber tree, the yielding work loop and the alternate-pointer swap are all implemented by hand.
The update queue is built, showing directly why an updater sees the pending value and a variable does not.

teaches.subtopic: The dispatcher, slot arrays and the rules of hooks
teaches.howCovered: useState and useEffect are implemented on an index-addressed array, deriving the rules rather than citing them.

teaches.subtopic: Why use() may be called conditionally
teaches.howCovered: With the slot array built, the exception for use() follows from it not being slot-backed.

teaches.subtopic: Why memo works and what it compares
teaches.howCovered: A bailout is added to the reconciler, making the shallow prop comparison something you wrote.

implicitFoundations.title: Cooperative scheduling
implicitFoundations.mechanism: requestIdleCallback and the 5ms frame budget let long work yield between units.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: This is the mechanism concurrent React generalises into lanes and priorities.

implicitFoundations.title: Double buffering
implicitFoundations.mechanism: Two fiber trees alternate; the previous tree is reused rather than reallocated.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Keeps allocation flat across renders, which is why React does not thrash the young generation.

implicitFoundations.title: The JSX transform
implicitFoundations.mechanism: Babel or the automatic runtime rewrites JSX into createElement or jsx() calls.
implicitFoundations.realWorldImpact: Makes clear that JSX is syntax over a function call, not a template language.

frameworkHandled: The JSX transform, configured to your own pragma

A test proving state follows keys and not positions.

The host-config boundary is the design: what belongs to the reconciler and what belongs to the DOM
The host config must handle real elements, attributes versus properties, and boolean attributes correctly
Controlled inputs are the hardest host-config case: value, defaultValue and the cursor position all interact
Focus must survive reconciliation, so a keyed reorder that steals focus is a renderer bug you have to fix
The demo fetches real data, so Suspense has something genuinely asynchronous to suspend on
The demo API is cross-origin, so the data layer running on the custom renderer faces real preflight
State persists across reload, which requires the renderer to hydrate an initial tree from storage
dangerouslySetInnerHTML is implemented, and naming it that is itself the lesson about untrusted markup
Style handling must respect which properties are unitless, or every layout value is silently wrong
The renderer appends px only to unitless numbers on the properties that accept it — a real, published list
Inline styles applied by the renderer sit above the cascade, which is why the style prop wins so often
The demo styles from data attributes the renderer writes, keeping DOM state and visual state in step
Focus, hover and disabled must all survive a keyed reorder, which is how renderer bugs surface visually
The demo is a grid-based layout, which stresses the host config with shorthand properties
Named grid areas exercise attribute-versus-property handling for hyphenated CSS names
Alignment shorthands are applied through the style prop, testing camelCase to kebab-case conversion
The toolbar is a flex row rendered entirely by the custom renderer
flex is a shorthand with a unitless first value, which is the exact case the px-appending rule must not break
Auto margins in the demo prove that layout behaves identically under a hand-written renderer
A portal renders into a different container, so the stacking context is decided by DOM position and not tree position
aspect-ratio takes a unitless value, another case the style handler must not append px to
Container queries are pure CSS, which is the cleanest demonstration of what the renderer does not have to do
Custom properties must bypass the camelCase transform entirely, since --my-token is already correct
